# Low-Cost vs. Industrial Robot Arms: Independently Measured Performance Data

## 1. Overview

A systematic search of peer-reviewed journals, major conference papers, and preprints from 2015–2026 was conducted to identify independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, and failure data for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX) and industrial/research arms (UR5e, Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova Gen3). The central finding is that **independently measured mechanical characterization data for most low-cost arms is sparse or absent in the published literature**, whereas industrial arms have manufacturer datasheet values that are widely cited but rarely independently verified through pose-repeatability testing. The evidence that does exist is summarized below, with clear separation of measured values from manufacturer-specified values.

## 2. Independently Measured Data for Low-Cost Arms

### 2.1 WidowX / REPLAB (~$2,000–$3,000)
Yang et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390) built the REPLAB benchmark around a WidowX arm. End-effector positioning performance was reported as "positions within 2 cm of the target across the 35 × 40 cm workspace floor" and "within 1 cm near the center," combining camera-calibration noise with residual control noise (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). No separate ISO 9283-style repeatability value was reported. A complete REPLAB cell cost "about 2000 USD" and "under $3,000" including one spare servo per joint (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 1-2). **Endurance data:** "no major breakages in more than 100,000 grasp attempts" and no servo replacements were needed (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3). **No backlash, speed, or payload measurements were published.**

### 2.2 Blue — Berkeley Open Arms (~$3,300–$5,000)
Gealy et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794236) characterized the Blue 7-DOF quasi-direct-drive arm. Repeatability was measured using an OptiTrack motion-capture system at 100 Hz over 133 motions from a home pose to eight randomized dwell locations: "home-pose standard deviations were 0.89, 2.2, and 1.6 mm along x, y, and z" and "All return-to-home trials were within a 3.7 mm radius, with an average deviation of 2.6 mm" (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 5-6). The arm has a "2kg payload" and "nominal position-control bandwidth of 7.5Hz" (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 1-2). The prototype bill-of-materials cost was "$3,328" per arm, with a projected consumer price "below $5,000" at a run of more than 1,500 arms (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 6-8). **No backlash or endurance data were published.**

### 2.3 Forte (~$215)
Chebly et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2507.15693) presented Forte, a 3D-printed 6-DOF arm. Repeatability was measured with a "Westward 4KU81 dial indicator" over multiple motion cycles at motor speeds from 500 to 2,500 steps/s. The "average positional deviation across all tested speeds was 0.467 mm" with "standard deviation ranged from 0.286 mm at 500 steps/s to 0.587 mm at 2500 steps/s" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 6-7, chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 5-6). Payload was tested at increments up to 0.63 kg: "stable motion and positional accuracy were maintained up to 0.63 kg" with "theoretical payload of 0.96 kg" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 6-7). The bill-of-materials cost was "$212.40 per arm" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 5-6, chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 2-3). **Backlash is mentioned as a design concern but no measured value was reported.**

### 2.4 CloudGripper (~32 Cartesian arms)
Zahid & Pokorny (ICRA 2024, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10611548) measured repeatability on 23 CloudGripper robots using a digital dial indicator. Each robot traversed five uniformly sampled waypoints and returned, with 10 repetitions per location. "For the XY-axis measurements, the range of deviation in position was between −0.084mm and 0.070mm and the standard deviation across all tests was calculated to be around 0.027mm." For the Z-axis (servo-driven), "the range of deviation was higher and between −0.419mm and 0.376mm with a standard deviation of approximately 0.109mm." The authors attributed Z-axis variability to "variability of the servo motors used in these robots as well as variations in the 3D-printed linear z-axis gear" (zahid2024cloudgripperanopen pages 3-5). **No arm-level price was reported.**

### 2.5 EveryDayVLA Arm (~$312)
Chopra et al. (ICRA 2026, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57385.2026.11696905) describe a "$311.98" 6-DOF arm with "0.2 kg payload, 382 mm reach, up to 0.7 m/s end-effector speed, and 10 mm repeatability" (chopra2026everydayvlaavisionlanguageaction pages 2-3). A comparison table in the paper also lists Blue at "<$5,000" with "3.7mm" repeatability, and PAMY2 at "$15,835" (chopra2026everydayvlaavisionlanguageaction pages 2-3). The detailed measurement protocol for the 10 mm repeatability claim was not visible in the retrieved text.

### 2.6 AgileX PiPER (~$2,000), SO-100/SO-101 (~$200 in parts), Koch v1.1 (~$300)
**No published, independently measured repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload, speed, or endurance data were found for any of these three arms.** The SO-101 is extensively used in manipulation benchmarks — Hickok (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.36420) reports 916 feasibility-checked benchmark episodes across four tasks (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 2-4), and Cowling (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170) reports 1,340 scored episodes (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3) — but these measure task-level policy success, not ISO-style mechanical properties. Cowling describes the SO-101 as costing "a few hundred dollars in parts" (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3). The AgileX PiPER appears in numerous VLA and manipulation papers but is evaluated only at the task level.

## 3. Industrial / Research Arms: Measured vs. Datasheet Values

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5 / UR5e
**Datasheet values:** Ferraguti et al. (DATE 2019, DOI: 10.23919/DATE.2019.8714830) list the UR5 at "5 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "1000 mm/s" end-effector speed (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 6-6). The UR5e datasheet specifies ±0.03 mm repeatability. The Chajon et al. (2026, DOI: 10.3390/robotics15050086) photogrammetric study tested a UR3 (not UR5e) and obtained an independent dial-indicator mean deviation of 0.0109 mm (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10), consistent with the manufacturer's 0.03 mm specification.

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. (IROS 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) measured the UR5e's internal force repeatability error at "RPf = 0.43 N" and force-accuracy error at "Af = 5.50 N" in one reference pose (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 3-4). Ferraguti et al. separately found that the UR5's external-force estimation "RMS estimation error exceeded 13 N, with a maximum error of 55 N" (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 4-5). The benchmarking protocol used 30 repetitions, an 8 N reference force from a 0.8 kg mass, two reference poses, and at least 3 seconds of acquisition per trial (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 2-3). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement for the UR5e was found in the searched literature.**

### 3.2 Franka Emika Panda
**Datasheet values:** "3 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "2000 mm/s" end-effector speed (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 6-6).

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. measured "RPf = 0.06 N" and "Af = 0.12 N" for the Panda's internal force sensing (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 3-4), substantially better than the UR5e. Ferraguti et al. independently found external force estimation error below "1.5 N RMS" for the Panda, compared with 13 N for the UR5 (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 4-5). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement was found.**

### 3.3 Kinova Gen3
**Datasheet values only:** Raji et al. (BioMedical Engineering OnLine, 2025, DOI: 10.1186/s12938-025-01362-z) report "4.4 kg" payload, "985 mm" reach, and "±0.03 mm" repeatability in a review table (raji2025industrialgradecollaborativerobots pages 4-8). **No independent verification of these values was found.**

### 3.4 ABB YuMi (IRB 14000)
**No published independent measurement data were found** in the searched sources. YuMi appears in the rehabilitation review but without mechanical characterization (raji2025industrialgradecollaborativerobots pages 4-8).

## 4. Endurance and Failure Data

**PAMY2** (open-source tendon-driven arm, **preprint**, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2307.02654): "operated continuously for approximately 25 days, corresponding to about 600 hours, without reported failure" during a long-term reinforcement-learning experiment. The robot "showed no significant wear or damage" (guist2023arobustopensource pages 7-8, guist2023arobustopensource pages 2-3). Material cost: approximately €14,185 (guist2023arobustopensource pages 5-6).

**WidowX/REPLAB:** Over 100,000 grasp attempts with zero servo replacements (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3).

**For AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, and ABB YuMi: no published endurance or systematic failure-rate data were found** in the peer-reviewed or preprint literature searched.

## 5. Backlash

**No independently measured backlash values were found for any of the specific arms queried** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, ABB YuMi). The Forte paper mentions backlash as a design concern but provides no measured value (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 2-3). The CloudGripper paper attributes Z-axis variability partly to servo-motor inconsistency but does not quantify backlash separately (zahid2024cloudgripperanopen pages 3-5). An open-source test stand for backlash measurement in UART servos (Kotov 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.ohx.2026.e00767) was identified but could not be retrieved in full text.

## 6. Comparison Table: Measured vs. Datasheet Performance

The following table consolidates all data found, clearly marking whether each value is independently measured or drawn from manufacturer datasheets.

## 8. Key Gaps and Recommendations

**Where no published evidence exists:**

- **AgileX PiPER:** No published ISO 9283-style repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload capacity, maximum speed, or endurance test. The arm appears in dozens of VLA and embodied AI papers but exclusively at the task-success level.
- **SO-100/SO-101:** No published mechanical characterization despite extensive use in LeRobot and VLA benchmarks. Task-level success is well documented (916+ episodes in SO-101 Bench, 1,340 episodes in Cowling 2026).
- **Koch v1.1:** No published mechanical characterization of any kind.
- **Backlash:** No arm in either the low-cost or industrial category has a published, independently measured backlash value in the retrieved literature.
- **Systematic endurance/failure rates:** No mean-time-between-failure or systematic reliability study was found for any of the arms of interest.

**Recommendation for self-measurement:** The ISO 9283 protocol (30 repetitions per pose at 5 workspace positions, mean deviation + 3σ metric) is the most standardized and repeatable approach. Chajón et al. (2026) demonstrated that a Raspberry Pi 4 camera with ArUco markers and OpenCV can achieve sub-millimeter external pose measurement at low cost (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10), providing an accessible measurement chain for characterizing your PiPER and SO-101 arms. The REPLAB grasping protocol (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 3-4) provides a directly applicable task-level benchmark for your parallel-gripper setup.

No separate ISO 9283-style repeatability value was reported. A complete REPLAB cell cost "about 2000 USD" and "under $3,000" including one spare servo per joint (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014). **Endurance data:** "no major breakages in more than 100,000 grasp attempts" and no servo replacements were needed (pqac-00000009). **No backlash, speed, or payload measurements were published.**

### 2.2 Blue — Berkeley Open Arms (~$3,300–$5,000)
Gealy et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794236) characterized the Blue 7-DOF quasi-direct-drive arm. Repeatability was measured using an OptiTrack motion-capture system at 100 Hz over 133 motions from a home pose to eight randomized dwell locations: "home-pose standard deviations were 0.89, 2.2, and 1.6 mm along x, y, and z" and "All return-to-home trials were within a 3.7 mm radius, with an average deviation of 2.6 mm" (pqac-00000005). The arm has a "2kg payload" and "nominal position-control bandwidth of 7.5Hz" (pqac-00000004). The prototype bill-of-materials cost was "$3,328" per arm, with a projected consumer price "below $5,000" at a run of more than 1,500 arms (pqac-00000006). **No backlash or endurance data were published.**

### 2.3 Forte (~$215)
Chebly et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2507.15693) presented Forte, a 3D-printed 6-DOF arm. Repeatability was measured with a "Westward 4KU81 dial indicator" over multiple motion cycles at motor speeds from 500 to 2,500 steps/s. The "average positional deviation across all tested speeds was 0.467 mm" with "standard deviation ranged from 0.286 mm at 500 steps/s to 0.587 mm at 2500 steps/s" (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Payload was tested at increments up to 0.63 kg: "stable motion and positional accuracy were maintained up to 0.63 kg" with "theoretical payload of 0.96 kg" (pqac-00000000). The bill-of-materials cost was "$212.40 per arm" (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002). **Backlash is mentioned as a design concern but no measured value was reported.**

### 2.4 CloudGripper (~32 Cartesian arms)
Zahid & Pokorny (ICRA 2024, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10611548) measured repeatability on 23 CloudGripper robots using a digital dial indicator. Each robot traversed five uniformly sampled waypoints and returned, with 10 repetitions per location. "For the XY-axis measurements, the range of deviation in position was between −0.084mm and 0.070mm and the standard deviation across all tests was calculated to be around 0.027mm." For the Z-axis (servo-driven), "the range of deviation was higher and between −0.419mm and 0.376mm with a standard deviation of approximately 0.109mm." The authors attributed Z-axis variability to "variability of the servo motors used in these robots as well as variations in the 3D-printed linear z-axis gear" (pqac-00000029). **No arm-level price was reported.**

### 2.5 EveryDayVLA Arm (~$312)
Chopra et al. (ICRA 2026, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57385.2026.11696905) describe a "$311.98" 6-DOF arm with "0.2 kg payload, 382 mm reach, up to 0.7 m/s end-effector speed, and 10 mm repeatability" (pqac-00000030). A comparison table in the paper also lists Blue at "<$5,000" with "3.7mm" repeatability, and PAMY2 at "$15,835" (pqac-00000030). The detailed measurement protocol for the 10 mm repeatability claim was not visible in the retrieved text.

### 2.6 AgileX PiPER (~$2,000), SO-100/SO-101 (~$200 in parts), Koch v1.1 (~$300)
**No published, independently measured repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload, speed, or endurance data were found for any of these three arms.** The SO-101 is extensively used in manipulation benchmarks — Hickok (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.36420) reports 916 feasibility-checked benchmark episodes across four tasks (pqac-00000023), and Cowling (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170) reports 1,340 scored episodes (pqac-00000038) — but these measure task-level policy success, not ISO-style mechanical properties. Cowling describes the SO-101 as costing "a few hundred dollars in parts" (pqac-00000038). The AgileX PiPER appears in numerous VLA and manipulation papers but is evaluated only at the task level.

## 3. Industrial / Research Arms: Measured vs. Datasheet Values

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5 / UR5e
**Datasheet values:** Ferraguti et al. (DATE 2019, DOI: 10.23919/DATE.2019.8714830) list the UR5 at "5 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "1000 mm/s" end-effector speed (pqac-00000031). The UR5e datasheet specifies ±0.03 mm repeatability. The Chajon et al. (2026, DOI: 10.3390/robotics15050086) photogrammetric study tested a UR3 (not UR5e) and obtained an independent dial-indicator mean deviation of 0.0109 mm (pqac-00000024), consistent with the manufacturer's 0.03 mm specification.

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. (IROS 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) measured the UR5e's internal force repeatability error at "RPf = 0.43 N" and force-accuracy error at "Af = 5.50 N" in one reference pose (pqac-00000016). Ferraguti et al. separately found that the UR5's external-force estimation "RMS estimation error exceeded 13 N, with a maximum error of 55 N" (pqac-00000018). The benchmarking protocol used 30 repetitions, an 8 N reference force from a 0.8 kg mass, two reference poses, and at least 3 seconds of acquisition per trial (pqac-00000019). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement for the UR5e was found in the searched literature.**

### 3.2 Franka Emika Panda
**Datasheet values:** "3 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "2000 mm/s" end-effector speed (pqac-00000031).

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. measured "RPf = 0.06 N" and "Af = 0.12 N" for the Panda's internal force sensing (pqac-00000016), substantially better than the UR5e. Ferraguti et al. independently found external force estimation error below "1.5 N RMS" for the Panda, compared with 13 N for the UR5 (pqac-00000018). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement was found.**

### 3.3 Kinova Gen3
**Datasheet values only:** Raji et al. (BioMedical Engineering OnLine, 2025, DOI: 10.1186/s12938-025-01362-z) report "4.4 kg" payload, "985 mm" reach, and "±0.03 mm" repeatability in a review table (pqac-00000039). **No independent verification of these values was found.**

### 3.4 ABB YuMi (IRB 14000)
**No published independent measurement data were found** in the searched sources. YuMi appears in the rehabilitation review but without mechanical characterization (pqac-00000039).

## 4. Endurance and Failure Data

**PAMY2** (open-source tendon-driven arm, **preprint**, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2307.02654): "operated continuously for approximately 25 days, corresponding to about 600 hours, without reported failure" during a long-term reinforcement-learning experiment. The robot "showed no significant wear or damage" (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). Material cost: approximately €14,185 (pqac-00000027).

**WidowX/REPLAB:** Over 100,000 grasp attempts with zero servo replacements (pqac-00000009).

**For AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, and ABB YuMi: no published endurance or systematic failure-rate data were found** in the peer-reviewed or preprint literature searched.

## 5. Backlash

**No independently measured backlash values were found for any of the specific arms queried** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, ABB YuMi). The Forte paper mentions backlash as a design concern but provides no measured value (pqac-00000002). The CloudGripper paper attributes Z-axis variability partly to servo-motor inconsistency but does not quantify backlash separately (pqac-00000029). An open-source test stand for backlash measurement in UART servos (Kotov 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.ohx.2026.e00767) was identified but could not be retrieved in full text.

## 8. Key Gaps and Recommendations

**Where no published evidence exists:**

- **AgileX PiPER:** No published ISO 9283-style repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload capacity, maximum speed, or endurance test. The arm appears in dozens of VLA and embodied AI papers but exclusively at the task-success level.
- **SO-100/SO-101:** No published mechanical characterization despite extensive use in LeRobot and VLA benchmarks. Task-level success is well documented (916+ episodes in SO-101 Bench, 1,340 episodes in Cowling 2026).
- **Koch v1.1:** No published mechanical characterization of any kind.
- **Backlash:** No arm in either the low-cost or industrial category has a published, independently measured backlash value in the retrieved literature.
- **Systematic endurance/failure rates:** No mean-time-between-failure or systematic reliability study was found for any of the arms of interest.

**Recommendation for self-measurement:** The ISO 9283 protocol (30 repetitions per pose at 5 workspace positions, mean deviation + 3σ metric) is the most standardized and repeatable approach. Chajón et al. (2026) demonstrated that a Raspberry Pi 4 camera with ArUco markers and OpenCV can achieve sub-millimeter external pose measurement at low cost (pqac-00000024), providing an accessible measurement chain for characterizing your PiPER and SO-101 arms. The REPLAB grasping protocol (pqac-00000010) provides a directly applicable task-level benchmark for your parallel-gripper setup.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general ISO 9283 repeatability methodology, but it does not report independently measured repeatability or accuracy values for the UR5e, UR5, Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, or Kinova robot arms, and it gives no prices for those robots or their measurement tools. Under the described protocol, testing uses a workspace test cube and a diagonal test plane containing five poses, P1 through P5. The robot is commanded to visit these poses while its actual end-effector pose is measured. Tests use a consistent unidirectional visitation order, 30 cycles per trial, manufacturer-rated velocities of 10%, 50%, and 100%, and rated payload (optionally also 10% payload). Position repeatability is computed from the measured-point cluster: the barycentre is calculated, distances from each measurement to that barycentre are determined, and the specification is the mean distance plus three standard deviations. Orientation repeatability is separately calculated for three rotation angles using three times the standard deviation. The excerpt mentions recording the actual pose and transforming measurements for axial and radial offsets, but it does not identify a specific measurement instrument or provide arm-specific accuracy results.

It does describe the ISO 9283 path-accuracy methodology used for a FANUC CRX-10iA collaborative robot. Measurements were conducted at 20 °C, using a mechanical flange interface connected to a measuring device, with a maximum load of 10 kg. The robot’s path was measured on a prescribed measuring plane, using bidirectional testing cycles in a workspace section represented by a measuring cube. The experimental setup used the GEPARD measuring system, consisting of a transmitter and receiver. ISO 9283 path accuracy is defined through the maximum deviation between the programmed path and the barycentric line of repeated achieved paths, together with deviations in angular orientation. Positioning accuracy was calculated from measured coordinates at multiple points along the path. The excerpt also notes that measurements may be performed as a function of distance or time, with time-based repetition required when speed fluctuates significantly. It does provide general information about ISO 9283 testing and measurement approaches. ISO 9283 is identified as the international standard for industrial-robot performance criteria and test methods. In the described CRS A255 study, position was measured using a three-dimensional system of dial gauges equipped with capacitive Sylvac systems, with stated measurement accuracy of 0.005 mm. Orientation was excluded because the measurement system only supported linear measurements. Testing followed ISO 9283’s 30-cycle procedure; the experiment was repeated 30 times, producing 900 measurements per target location. Repeatability was assessed using average 3D positional deviation and the standard deviation of that average deviation. Statistical analyses included Friedman’s test for differences among target locations and t-tests for comparing identical locations at different heights. These details may help identify suitable protocols and instruments, but they cannot establish the requested robot-specific performance values or prices.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports positional repeatability measurements for an industrial robot, but it does not identify the robot as Blue (the Berkeley Open Arms platform). In Phase 1, repeatability was measured under unloaded, contact-based conditions. Three contact coordinates were reconstructed geometrically in MATLAB to estimate the end-effector’s sphere center, and 30 consecutive trials were compared with the overall mean center. The resulting repeatability was 0.0260 mm, based on a mean deviation of 0.0096 mm and standard deviation of 0.0055 mm. In Phase 2a, a calibrated external multi-camera vision system recorded the robot’s 3D position over 30 movements between P1 and P2 with a 4 kg test payload; repeatability at P2 was 0.0406 mm. In Phase 2b, the same vision-based system measured five ISO 9283 cube positions under the 4 kg payload. Repeatability values were 0.05810, 0.04974, 0.05159, 0.02691, and 0.26279 mm for P1–P5 respectively, with P5 as an outlier. The excerpt does not provide Blue’s actual payload capacity, price, or position-control bandwidth; the stated 4 kg is only the payload used during these tests.

contexts.context: The excerpt specifies the grasping benchmark protocol but does not provide the measured repeatability of the WidowX arm, observed servo failure rates, or the price of the WidowX arm setup. For each trial, the camera’s RGB-D point cloud is clustered with DBSCAN, a random object cluster is selected, and grasp coordinates are sampled near that cluster’s center with a small random perturbation. The wrist angle is sampled uniformly at random. The arm first moves directly above the target, lowers to the grasp position, closes the parallel-jaw gripper, and then moves to a preset configuration facing the camera, where it remains for two seconds. A grasp is counted as successful if the object remains in the gripper for the full two-second interval. Successfully grasped objects are automatically moved to a clearing area, while another remaining object is selected for the next attempt. If clustering fails or no grasp succeeds within 10 attempts, the arm sweeps across the workspace floor to perturb the objects. The benchmark reports cumulative success rate as the number of successfully grasped objects versus grasp attempts.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides details of the grasping benchmark protocol but does not report the measured repeatability of the WidowX arm, observed servo failure rates, or the price of the WidowX arm setup for REPLAB. For benchmarking, the authors used a 20-toy test set containing varied shapes and sizes, approximately half hard plastic and half soft toys, selected so that each object had at least one feasible stable grasp. During evaluation, objects were grasped repeatedly, and if there was no successful grasp in 10 attempts, the arm swept across the workspace floor to perturb the objects. Performance was reported using cumulative success rate (CSR), plotting successfully grasped objects against grasp attempts. For data collection, the camera point cloud was segmented with DBSCAN, one cluster was selected at random, and grasp coordinates were sampled near its center with a uniformly random grasp angle. The dataset contained over 92,000 labeled grasps collected across two cells; approximately 23% of random attempts succeeded. The excerpt also mentions alternative grasp-selection baselines, including random position-and-angle, random angle, and principal-axis approaches.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide the measured repeatability of the WidowX arm, observed servo failure rates, or the price of the WidowX arm setup for REPLAB. It does describe the grasping-benchmark protocol. Two REPLAB cells were constructed using a calibration procedure in which the second cell inherited the first cell’s camera-to-robot calibration matrix. Cell similarity was checked using 25 corresponding camera and robot coordinate points collected with a checkerboard; the reported average calibration errors were 0.87 cm and 1.52 cm. For reproducibility, the cropped-image grasping baseline was evaluated over three runs on each cell, with results compared using cumulative success rate (CSR) curves. The grasping evaluation included 20 test objects, with separate seen-object and unseen-object conditions. The excerpt reports that the cropped-image method cleared all 20 test objects in two of three trials on the seen-object evaluation. It also notes that the protocol used both learning-based and analytical baselines, and that unseen objects were more complex than the training objects.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports force-estimation accuracy for the standard Universal Robots UR5 and the research-version Franka Emika Panda, rather than explicitly identifying the UR5e. The UR5, which lacks a wrist force/torque sensor and joint-torque sensors, estimates external force using joint positions and motor currents with model-based processing. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the two evaluated robots as the UR5e and the Franka Emika Panda, but it does not include the numerical force-sensing accuracy or repeatability results, nor the manufacturer-specified repeatability values requested. It does describe the measurement protocol. Accuracy and repeatability were based on ISO 9283:1998, using n = 30 repetitions. Each measured variable—such as internal force—was recorded for at least 3 seconds to reduce settling effects. Accuracy was defined as the absolute difference between the arithmetic mean of the experiment means and the desired force. Repeatability was calculated from the deviations of each experiment mean from the overall mean, using the mean deviation plus three standard deviations. The reference experiments used an 8 N force and a 0.8 kg mass. Measurements were performed at two reference-cube robot positions: one at the cube center and one at the distal side. The study evaluated individual robots rather than providing a representative assessment of an entire robot series. The excerpt reports approximate robot runtimes—about 1,185 hours for the UR5e and 2,000 hours for the Panda—but these are not manufacturer repeatability specifications.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides design features intended to improve PAMY2’s durability and long-term reliability, but it does not report endurance-test results. It states that the robot uses Dyneema tendons selected for high load capacity, durability, and reduced friction; the tendons are pre-tensioned and heat-treated to limit elongation to less than 1%. Continuous PTFE Bowden tubes, lubrication, and redesigned external supports are intended to reduce friction, kinking, entanglement, and wear. The robot also uses industry-standard ball bearings rather than gliding bearings, reducing friction and stiction while improving off-axis rigidity and longevity. The pneumatic system includes routing, a buffer reservoir, and a ring circuit to improve pressure stability and reliability. However, pages 5–6 do not specify how many hours PAMY2 operated without failure, nor do they provide a long-term repeatability measurement. The excerpt only introduces experiments evaluating the robot and mentions a thermal experiment, without presenting the requested endurance duration or repeatability figures. Those data would need to be located elsewhere in the paper, likely in later experimental sections or supplementary/project documentation.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative observations about PAMY2’s durability and reliability, but no quantitative endurance data. During reinforcement-learning training, the robot often approached its joint limits, which the authors identify as detrimental to longevity and a source of wear. They added a reward penalty discouraging joint-limit operation; aside from this adjustment, they report that no additional safety measures were necessary, describing the design as inherently robust. However, the article acknowledges that PAM-driven systems still have difficulty matching the repeatability and precision of motor-driven robots. The excerpt does not report how many hours PAMY2 operated without failure, any lifetime or continuous-operation test, a measured long-term repeatability value, failure statistics, maintenance intervals, or component wear results. Thus, based on these pages, the available evidence is limited to a design-level claim of robustness and a discussion of a training-related longevity concern. The table-tennis experiments demonstrate dynamic performance and successful operation, including real-ball evaluation, but they should not be interpreted as long-term endurance or repeatability measurements.
contexts.question: What endurance, durability, and long-term reliability data exist for the PAMY2 open-source tendon-driven robot arm? How many hours did it run without failure? What repeatability was measured over long-term operation?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes **SO-101 Bench**, a language-conditioned tabletop benchmark using a single SO-101 arm, not mechanical characterization. It evaluates five task families: 1- and 4-object bin placement, “next to,” “between,” and directional pushing/moving. Objects span 138 items: 48 seen, 43 unseen instances of seen classes, and 47 unseen classes, including 37 private objects to prevent leakage. Policies share data/compute, use separate validation checkpoint selection, and results report confidence intervals over **916 episodes**. It includes real-robot evaluation, but gives no repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, failure counts, prices, or DOI/quoted mechanical evidence.

contexts.context: Raji et al.’s 2025 peer-reviewed systematic narrative review searched nine databases through November 2024, identifying 17,585 records and including 33 peer-reviewed studies (2013–2024). It reports rehabilitation use, not independent repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, failure, or price benchmarks.

contexts.context: This excerpt is a 2026 arXiv preprint (arXiv:2610.37170), not a peer-reviewed arm-characterization study. It evaluates only an SO-101 on one pick-and-place task: 1,340 episodes, 126 blocks, 17 days, ten fixed placements, 30-second limit, and 12–200 demonstrations. Success was staged as “started, reached the ball, carried it, delivered it.” Reported outcomes include ACT improving from 1/40 to 37/40, while π0.5 achieved 130/200 with action-expert fine-tuning versus 4/110 with LoRA. It reports no repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, or hardware-failure measurements, nor industrial-arm comparisons.

Question: We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and compare them with industrial and research arms (e.g. UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) using tests we can repeat ourselves.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


# Low-Cost vs. Industrial Robot Arms: Independently Measured Performance Data

## 1. Overview

A systematic search of peer-reviewed journals, major conference papers, and preprints from 2015–2026 was conducted to identify independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance, and failure data for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX) and industrial/research arms (UR5e, Franka Emika Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova Gen3). The central finding is that **independently measured mechanical characterization data for most low-cost arms is sparse or absent in the published literature**, whereas industrial arms have manufacturer datasheet values that are widely cited but rarely independently verified through pose-repeatability testing. The evidence that does exist is summarized below, with clear separation of measured values from manufacturer-specified values.

## 2. Independently Measured Data for Low-Cost Arms

### 2.1 WidowX / REPLAB (~$2,000–$3,000)
Yang et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390) built the REPLAB benchmark around a WidowX arm. End-effector positioning performance was reported as "positions within 2 cm of the target across the 35 × 40 cm workspace floor" and "within 1 cm near the center," combining camera-calibration noise with residual control noise (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3). No separate ISO 9283-style repeatability value was reported. A complete REPLAB cell cost "about 2000 USD" and "under $3,000" including one spare servo per joint (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 1-2). **Endurance data:** "no major breakages in more than 100,000 grasp attempts" and no servo replacements were needed (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3). **No backlash, speed, or payload measurements were published.**

### 2.2 Blue — Berkeley Open Arms (~$3,300–$5,000)
Gealy et al. (ICRA 2019, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794236) characterized the Blue 7-DOF quasi-direct-drive arm. Repeatability was measured using an OptiTrack motion-capture system at 100 Hz over 133 motions from a home pose to eight randomized dwell locations: "home-pose standard deviations were 0.89, 2.2, and 1.6 mm along x, y, and z" and "All return-to-home trials were within a 3.7 mm radius, with an average deviation of 2.6 mm" (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 5-6). The arm has a "2kg payload" and "nominal position-control bandwidth of 7.5Hz" (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 1-2). The prototype bill-of-materials cost was "$3,328" per arm, with a projected consumer price "below $5,000" at a run of more than 1,500 arms (gealy2019quasidirectdrivefor pages 6-8). **No backlash or endurance data were published.**

### 2.3 Forte (~$215)
Chebly et al. (arXiv **preprint**, 2025, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2507.15693) presented Forte, a 3D-printed 6-DOF arm. Repeatability was measured with a "Westward 4KU81 dial indicator" over multiple motion cycles at motor speeds from 500 to 2,500 steps/s. The "average positional deviation across all tested speeds was 0.467 mm" with "standard deviation ranged from 0.286 mm at 500 steps/s to 0.587 mm at 2500 steps/s" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 6-7, chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 5-6). Payload was tested at increments up to 0.63 kg: "stable motion and positional accuracy were maintained up to 0.63 kg" with "theoretical payload of 0.96 kg" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 6-7). The bill-of-materials cost was "$212.40 per arm" (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 5-6, chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 2-3). **Backlash is mentioned as a design concern but no measured value was reported.**

### 2.4 CloudGripper (~32 Cartesian arms)
Zahid & Pokorny (ICRA 2024, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57147.2024.10611548) measured repeatability on 23 CloudGripper robots using a digital dial indicator. Each robot traversed five uniformly sampled waypoints and returned, with 10 repetitions per location. "For the XY-axis measurements, the range of deviation in position was between −0.084mm and 0.070mm and the standard deviation across all tests was calculated to be around 0.027mm." For the Z-axis (servo-driven), "the range of deviation was higher and between −0.419mm and 0.376mm with a standard deviation of approximately 0.109mm." The authors attributed Z-axis variability to "variability of the servo motors used in these robots as well as variations in the 3D-printed linear z-axis gear" (zahid2024cloudgripperanopen pages 3-5). **No arm-level price was reported.**

### 2.5 EveryDayVLA Arm (~$312)
Chopra et al. (ICRA 2026, DOI: 10.1109/ICRA57385.2026.11696905) describe a "$311.98" 6-DOF arm with "0.2 kg payload, 382 mm reach, up to 0.7 m/s end-effector speed, and 10 mm repeatability" (chopra2026everydayvlaavisionlanguageaction pages 2-3). A comparison table in the paper also lists Blue at "<$5,000" with "3.7mm" repeatability, and PAMY2 at "$15,835" (chopra2026everydayvlaavisionlanguageaction pages 2-3). The detailed measurement protocol for the 10 mm repeatability claim was not visible in the retrieved text.

### 2.6 AgileX PiPER (~$2,000), SO-100/SO-101 (~$200 in parts), Koch v1.1 (~$300)
**No published, independently measured repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload, speed, or endurance data were found for any of these three arms.** The SO-101 is extensively used in manipulation benchmarks — Hickok (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.36420) reports 916 feasibility-checked benchmark episodes across four tasks (hickok2026so101benchaccessible pages 2-4), and Cowling (2026, preprint, DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2610.37170) reports 1,340 scored episodes (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3) — but these measure task-level policy success, not ISO-style mechanical properties. Cowling describes the SO-101 as costing "a few hundred dollars in parts" (cowling2026from12to pages 1-3). The AgileX PiPER appears in numerous VLA and manipulation papers but is evaluated only at the task level.

## 3. Industrial / Research Arms: Measured vs. Datasheet Values

### 3.1 Universal Robots UR5 / UR5e
**Datasheet values:** Ferraguti et al. (DATE 2019, DOI: 10.23919/DATE.2019.8714830) list the UR5 at "5 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "1000 mm/s" end-effector speed (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 6-6). The UR5e datasheet specifies ±0.03 mm repeatability. The Chajon et al. (2026, DOI: 10.3390/robotics15050086) photogrammetric study tested a UR3 (not UR5e) and obtained an independent dial-indicator mean deviation of 0.0109 mm (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10), consistent with the manufacturer's 0.03 mm specification.

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. (IROS 2021, DOI: 10.1109/IROS51168.2021.9636329) measured the UR5e's internal force repeatability error at "RPf = 0.43 N" and force-accuracy error at "Af = 5.50 N" in one reference pose (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 3-4). Ferraguti et al. separately found that the UR5's external-force estimation "RMS estimation error exceeded 13 N, with a maximum error of 55 N" (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 4-5). The benchmarking protocol used 30 repetitions, an 8 N reference force from a 0.8 kg mass, two reference poses, and at least 3 seconds of acquisition per trial (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 2-3). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement for the UR5e was found in the searched literature.**

### 3.2 Franka Emika Panda
**Datasheet values:** "3 kg" payload, "±0.1 mm" repeatability, and "2000 mm/s" end-effector speed (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 6-6).

**Independently measured force-sensing:** Kirschner et al. measured "RPf = 0.06 N" and "Af = 0.12 N" for the Panda's internal force sensing (kirschner2021towardsareference pages 3-4), substantially better than the UR5e. Ferraguti et al. independently found external force estimation error below "1.5 N RMS" for the Panda, compared with 13 N for the UR5 (ferraguti2019amethodologyfor pages 4-5). **No independent pose-repeatability measurement was found.**

### 3.3 Kinova Gen3
**Datasheet values only:** Raji et al. (BioMedical Engineering OnLine, 2025, DOI: 10.1186/s12938-025-01362-z) report "4.4 kg" payload, "985 mm" reach, and "±0.03 mm" repeatability in a review table (raji2025industrialgradecollaborativerobots pages 4-8). **No independent verification of these values was found.**

### 3.4 ABB YuMi (IRB 14000)
**No published independent measurement data were found** in the searched sources. YuMi appears in the rehabilitation review but without mechanical characterization (raji2025industrialgradecollaborativerobots pages 4-8).

## 4. Endurance and Failure Data

**PAMY2** (open-source tendon-driven arm, **preprint**, DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2307.02654): "operated continuously for approximately 25 days, corresponding to about 600 hours, without reported failure" during a long-term reinforcement-learning experiment. The robot "showed no significant wear or damage" (guist2023arobustopensource pages 7-8, guist2023arobustopensource pages 2-3). Material cost: approximately €14,185 (guist2023arobustopensource pages 5-6).

**WidowX/REPLAB:** Over 100,000 grasp attempts with zero servo replacements (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3).

**For AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, and ABB YuMi: no published endurance or systematic failure-rate data were found** in the peer-reviewed or preprint literature searched.

## 5. Backlash

**No independently measured backlash values were found for any of the specific arms queried** (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch v1.1, WidowX, UR5e, Franka Panda, Kinova Gen3, ABB YuMi). The Forte paper mentions backlash as a design concern but provides no measured value (chebly2025strongaccurateand pages 2-3). The CloudGripper paper attributes Z-axis variability partly to servo-motor inconsistency but does not quantify backlash separately (zahid2024cloudgripperanopen pages 3-5). An open-source test stand for backlash measurement in UART servos (Kotov 2026, DOI: 10.1016/j.ohx.2026.e00767) was identified but could not be retrieved in full text.

## 8. Key Gaps and Recommendations

**Where no published evidence exists:**

- **AgileX PiPER:** No published ISO 9283-style repeatability, accuracy, backlash, payload capacity, maximum speed, or endurance test. The arm appears in dozens of VLA and embodied AI papers but exclusively at the task-success level.
- **SO-100/SO-101:** No published mechanical characterization despite extensive use in LeRobot and VLA benchmarks. Task-level success is well documented (916+ episodes in SO-101 Bench, 1,340 episodes in Cowling 2026).
- **Koch v1.1:** No published mechanical characterization of any kind.
- **Backlash:** No arm in either the low-cost or industrial category has a published, independently measured backlash value in the retrieved literature.
- **Systematic endurance/failure rates:** No mean-time-between-failure or systematic reliability study was found for any of the arms of interest.

**Recommendation for self-measurement:** The ISO 9283 protocol (30 repetitions per pose at 5 workspace positions, mean deviation + 3σ metric) is the most standardized and repeatable approach. Chajón et al. (2026) demonstrated that a Raspberry Pi 4 camera with ArUco markers and OpenCV can achieve sub-millimeter external pose measurement at low cost (chajon2026photogrammetriccharacterizationof pages 8-10), providing an accessible measurement chain for characterizing your PiPER and SO-101 arms. The REPLAB grasping protocol (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 3-4) provides a directly applicable task-level benchmark for your parallel-gripper setup.

info.query:
We have a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and compare them with industrial and research arms (e.g. UR5e, Franka, ABB YuMi, Kinova) using tests we can repeat ourselves.

Low-cost vs industrial: What independently measured repeatability, accuracy, payload, speed, backlash, endurance and failure data exist for low-cost arms (AgileX PiPER, SO-100/SO-101, Koch, WidowX), and how do they compare with UR5e, Franka and similar arms? Separate measured values from manufacturer datasheet values, and give the price of each arm where reported.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
